title: A neural theory of binocular rivalry
summary: Laing and Chow develop a biophysically-grounded spiking and rate-model account of binocular rivalry in which two populations of cortical neurons, each selective for one eye's image, mutually inhibit one another via shared inhibitory interneurons. Slow spike-frequency adaptation (and/or synaptic depression) within the currently dominant population gradually weakens its drive, allowing the suppressed population to escape inhibition and take over. This reciprocal-inhibition + adaptation circuit motif reproduces the stochastic alternations, gamma-like dominance durations, and Levelt's propositions observed psychophysically, and has since become the canonical circuit explanation for perceptual rivalry.
key_findings: Two excitatory populations encoding the rival monocular images compete through cross-inhibition mediated by inhibitory interneurons in early visual cortex.
Spike-frequency adaptation (calcium-activated K+ currents) in the dominant population acts as the slow fatigue variable that triggers switches.
Noise in the network sets the stochastic distribution of dominance durations, yielding the gamma-shaped histograms seen experimentally.
The model captures Levelt's propositions: increasing contrast to one eye shortens the dominance of the *other* eye rather than lengthening the stimulated eye's dominance.
Establishes the general 'competition + adaptation + noise' circuit motif now used to model perceptual multistability more broadly.
